newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader renews independence vow.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader renews independence vow.

text.p: Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov renewed a pledge to win independence from Russia in a speech on Sunday marking the 53rd anniversary of Stalin's deportation of the entire Chechen nation during World War Two.
Maskhadov, who was elected with a huge majority a month ago, said: "I fully intend building an independent state."
He was addressing a crowd of several hundred at a recently rebuilt memorial to the victims of the deporation in the war-ravaged Chechen capital, Grozny.

Moscow, which pulled out its troops last autumn after a bloody but unsuccessful two-year intervention against separatist rebels, refuses to countenance Chechen sovereignty. Negotiations are continuing between the two sides.

Chechnya needs massive investment to rebuild its economy and housing after the war, which killed tens of thousands. It will have to rely mainly on Moscow as foreign states are unlikely to risk Russia's wrath by recognising Grozny's independence.
Stalin accused the million-strong Chechen nation and other mainly Moslem North Caucasus peoples of aiding the invading German army. He ordered them to be deported en masse in 1944.
Tens of thousands died in transit and on the bleak steppes of Kazakhstan, where they were dumped and forced to fend for themselves.
After Stalin's death in 1953, the Chechens were allowed to return home but memories of the deportation are still vivid and helped stiffen resistance to Russia during the war.
Polish television aired an interview on Saturday with maverick Chechen guerrilla Salman Raduyev in which he repeated a threat to attack Russian cities in April.

Raduyev, who made his name with a bloody hostage-taking raid in the Russian province of Dagestan, which borders Chechnya, in January 1996, said he would destroy several Russian towns on April 21, first anniversary of a Russian attack against former Chechen rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev.
Raduyev denies the Chechen leadership's assertions that Dudayev died that day and does not recognise Maskhadov's rule.
"We are declaring April 21 a day of national revenge," he said in the interview, recorded two weeks ago. "At least three Russian towns will go up in smoke...Revenge is inevitable."

On January 29, two days after Maskhadov was elected on a pledge to bring Chechnya's fighters under control, Raduyev told Reuters he was mounting "Operation Ash", to destroy at least three Russian cities.
But there is no evidence that Raduyev, who espouses a particularly fiery brand of fundamentalist Islam, is in a position to carry out that threat.
